response.answer: Based on the most recent data, Yayoi Kusama, the renowned Japanese artist known for her iconic polka dot works and immersive installations, passed away at the age of 97. Her exhibitions, such as the Infinity Mirror Rooms at the Tate Modern, have been highly acclaimed and visited extensively. Kusama's career saw a resurgence in her 80s and 90s, after facing challenges in the masculine-dominated art scene of New York in the 1960s. Her work continues to be celebrated globally, with her retrospective at Hong Kong’s M+ Museum in 2022 being the largest comprehensive survey of her work in Asia outside Japan.

She returned to Japan and checked herself into a psychiatric hospital in Tokyo in 1977 that offered art therapy. # Japanese polka dot artist Yayoi Kusama dies aged 97

Reuters Japanese artist Yayoi Kusama poses for a photograph inside her Infinity Mirrored Room installation titled "The Souls of Millions of Light Years Away" during a media preview of her new exhibition at the David Zwirner gallery in New York, U.S.

Japanese avant-garde artist Yayoi Kusama, who became famous for her colourful polka dot-covered sculptures and installations, has died at the age of 97. [...] Catherine Wood, interim director of Tate Modern, told BBC Radio 4's Today programme on Thursday it was "our most visited exhibition of all time because people really love Kusama's work".

The exhibition invited visitors into the artist's Infinity Mirror Rooms.

"You would step in there and the lights would go down, and it felt like you were looking into the mysteries of the Universe," Wood said. "She was very good at conjuring this sense of wonder and infinity that she was obsessed with." [...] Kusama became one of the world's most recognisable artists and a global cultural icon in her 80s and 90s, after having been mostly overlooked for decades.

Poorly received by a masculine-dominated art scene of New York in the 1960s, Kusama caused a stir with her exhibitions of phallic sculptures, including a fabric couch, and frequent displays of nudity.

NY Daily News via Getty Images Yayoi Kusama paints body of Kent Feathergill, 1967.

# Yayoi Kusama, Japan’s ‘queen of polka dots’, dies at 97

Kusama turned her hallucinations into work that ranged from dot-covered paintings and pumpkin sculptures to infinity mirror room installations.

Save

Share

FILE PHOTO: Japanese artist Yayoi Kusama poses for a photograph inside her Infinity Mirrored Room installation titled [...] Japanese artist Yayoi Kusama in her Infinity Mirrored Room installation titled 'The Souls of Millions of Light Years Away' [File: Mike Segar/Reuters]



By Al Jazeera Staff, AP and Reuters

Published On 27 Aug 202627 Aug 2026

Yayoi Kusama, the Japanese artist known for her polka-dot paintings, pumpkin sculptures and immersive “Infinity Mirror Rooms”, has died at the age of 97. [...] As her fame grew, her international exhibitions attracted huge crowds and her works commanded lofty prices. One painting, Untitled (Nets) (1959), sold for $10.5m in 2022.

She received the Order of Culture, Japan’s highest honour for artists, in 2016.

David Zwirner, an art dealer who represented Kusama for 15 years, said she “was without a doubt the most famous living artist in the world” at the time of her passing.

results.title: Opinion | Yayoi Kusama’s Fame Eclipsed Her Art
results.content:
In 1988, when I met her, Yayoi Kusama had been living in a psychiatric hospital in Tokyo for over a decade, and was nearly forgotten by the art world in New York. As a graduate student researching postwar Japanese art, I had been invited to curate the opening exhibition at a new institution in New York, the Center for International Contemporary Arts (CICA). I chose Ms. Kusama, with the ambition to wrest her from obscurity. [...] Supported by

Guest Essay

# She Changed the World From an Asylum in Tokyo

By Alexandra Munroe

Ms. Munroe is a writer and senior curator at the Guggenheim Museum and organized Yayoi Kusama’s first retrospective exhibition.
